issue.issue_text: Whether the protection under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is available to a public servant accused of cheating by drawing false Travelling Allowance (T.A.) bills, on the grounds that the act was committed in the discharge of official duty.

facts: A public servant (appellant), working as a Regional Officer, was prosecuted for the offence of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
The allegation was that he submitted false Travelling Allowance (T.A.) bills, including claims for airfare he was not entitled to, and received payment for them.
The appellant argued that the prosecution could not proceed without a prior sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the act was committed in his capacity as a public officer.
law: Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires prior sanction from the government to prosecute a public servant for an offence committed 'while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty'.
The protection is not available for every offence committed by a public servant. The key test is whether the act complained of is 'directly and reasonably connected' with their official duties.
If the official status merely provides the 'occasion or opportunity' for the commission of the offence, rather than being an integral part of the duty, the protection of Section 197 does not apply.

The court cited precedent establishing that certain offences, such as cheating, by their very nature, cannot be regarded as having been committed by a public servant while acting in the discharge of their official duty.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished between the appellant's official duties as a Regional Officer and the act of drawing T.A. bills.
It held that while the appellant's status as a public servant authorized him to draw such bills, the act of drawing them was not his official duty.
The court reasoned that the act of cheating by submitting false bills was not 'directly and reasonably connected' with his duties as a Regional Officer.
Instead, his official status merely 'furnished the opportunity' for him to commit the offence of cheating.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the act of cheating by submitting false T.A. bills was not an act committed while discharging or purporting to discharge an official duty. Therefore, the protection under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not available to the appellant, and no prior sanction was required for his prosecution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the protection under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is available to a public servant accused of cheating by drawing false Travelling Allowance (T.A.) bills, on the grounds that the act was committed in the discharge of official duty.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the act of submitting the impugned T.A. bills and drawing the allowance was done in their capacity as a public officer.
It was argued that furnishing the bills and drawing the allowance were integrally connected with the appellant's status as a public servant.
Therefore, the act should be considered as being done while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty, thus requiring prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's specific arguments are not detailed in the provided text.

cases.case_name: K. Satwant Singh v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: That where a public servant commits the offence of cheating, the offence is not one committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, as the official status merely furnishes the occasion or opportunity for the commission of the offence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a public servant commits an offense, such as cheating, that has no necessary connection to the performance of their duties, the offense is not considered to be committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. If the official status merely furnishes the occasion or opportunity for the commission of the offense, the protection from prosecution without prior sanction under Section 197 of the Code is not available.
obiter: The prosecution was laid about 8 years back and on the plea of want of sanction the matter has been dragged on for such a long time at different stages.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the act of drawing false Travelling Allowance (T.A.) bills is not an act committed in the discharge of official duty. While the appellant's status as a public servant authorized him to draw such bills, the act of drawing them was not directly and reasonably connected with his specific duties as a Regional Officer. Instead, his official status merely furnished the opportunity for committing the acts that constitute the ingredients of the offence of cheating, and therefore, he was not entitled to the protection of prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
legal_tests_applied: The sine qua non for the applicability of this section is that the offence charged, be it one of commission or omission, must be one which has been committed by the public servant either in his official capacity or under colour of the office held by him.

If the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties attaching to the office as to be inseparable from them, then sanction under s.197(1) would be necessary; but if there was no necessary connection between them and the-performance of those duties, the official status furnishing only the occasion or opportunity for the acts, then no sanction would be required.

It is not every offence committed by a public servant that requires sanction for prosecution under section 197 (I) of the Code of Criminal Procedure; nor even every act done by him while he is actually engaged in the performance of his official duties; but if the act complained of is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office, then sanction would be necessary.
The test may well be whether the public servant, if challenged, can reasonably claim that, what he does in virtue of his office.
why_appellant_lost: The Court held that the offence of cheating has no necessary connection with the performance of the duties of a public servant.
It was not contended, nor was it the case, that the official duty of the appellant was to draw travelling allowance bills.
The act of drawing T.A. bills was not directly and reasonably connected with the appellant's duty as a Regional Officer of the Directorate.
The appellant's official status merely furnished the opportunity for doing the acts which constitute the ingredients of the offence, which is insufficient to invoke the protection of Section 197.
why_respondent_won: The Court affirmed the legal principle that where a public servant commits the offence of cheating, the offence is not one committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty.
The Court found that there was no necessary connection between the act of submitting false T.A. bills and the performance of the appellant's official duties.
The Court concluded that the official status of the accused only provided the occasion or opportunity for the commission of the offence, which does not meet the legal test for requiring sanction.
policy_considerations: The section is designed to facilitate an effective and unhampered performance of official duty by public servants by making provision for scrutiny into allegations against them by superior authorities and prior sanction for prosecution as a condition precedent to the cognizance of cases against them by courts so that protection may be available from frivolous, vexatious or false prosecutions for offences alleged to have been committed by them while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.
